meta.title: [IRS] Midterm — 60 Unique Questions
meta.description: Comprehensive midterm set covering evaluation, retrieval models, index compression, text processing, and OpenSearch.

questions.questionMd: The Soundex algorithm is best described as a tool designed for which specific purpose?

options.label: A
options.text: Ranking spelling correction candidates by their edit distance from a misspelled query

options.label: B
options.text: Wildcard query resolution by hashing vocabulary terms into fixed-length codes

options.label: C
options.text: Phonetic matching of proper names by encoding names that sound similar to the same code

options.label: D
options.text: General-purpose spelling correction for any English vocabulary term

questions.explanationMd: Soundex is a phonetic encoding method mainly used to match names that sound alike even when they are spelled differently.

questions.questionMd: A term has high TF in a document but very low IDF across the collection. What does this combination indicate about the term's usefulness as a relevance signal?

options.label: A
options.text: The term should be removed from the index because its combined TF-IDF weight will be exactly zero

options.label: B
options.text: The term is a weak discriminator because it appears frequently in many documents

options.label: C
options.text: The term is a strong relevance signal because high TF always dominates the combined TF-IDF weight

options.label: D
options.text: The term is highly informative because low IDF indicates it appears in very few documents

questions.explanationMd: Low IDF means the term occurs in many documents, so even if it is frequent in one document it is not very discriminative for relevance.

questions.questionMd: Three queries yield Average Precision scores of `0.72`, `0.45`, and `0.38` for a system. What is the MAP?

options.label: A
options.text: 0.550, computed as the median of the three AP values

options.label: B
options.text: 0.720, because MAP reports the highest AP score across all queries

options.label: D
options.text: 1.550, because MAP sums the AP values without dividing by the number of queries

questions.explanationMd: MAP is the mean of Average Precision values over all queries: `(0.72 + 0.45 + 0.38) / 3 = 0.5167`, approximately `0.517`.

questions.questionMd: The NLTK English stopword list contains approximately how many words, and what is the approximate size of Lucene's default stopword list?

options.label: A
options.text: 500 words in NLTK and approximately 100 in Lucene

options.label: B
options.text: 179 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene

options.label: C
options.text: 33 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene

options.label: D
options.text: 179 words in NLTK and approximately 33 in Lucene

questions.explanationMd: The lecture comparison uses about `179` English stopwords for NLTK and about `33` default stopwords for Lucene.

questions.questionMd: In SMART notation, what does the scheme `lnc` specify for document weighting?

options.label: A
options.text: Log-average TF, natural IDF, no normalization

options.label: B
options.text: Logarithmic TF, no IDF, cosine normalization

options.label: C
options.text: Logarithmic TF, natural IDF, cosine normalization

options.label: D
options.text: Natural TF, no IDF, cosine normalization

questions.explanationMd: In SMART notation, `l` means logarithmic term frequency, `n` means no IDF, and `c` means cosine normalization.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture's compression data, combining gap encoding with VB encoding on a typical postings list achieves what overall compression factor compared to storing raw `int32` document IDs?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 3-5x compression

options.label: B
options.text: Exactly 8x compression because VB uses 7 data bits per byte instead of 8

options.label: C
options.text: Less than 1.5x compression

options.label: D
options.text: Approximately 10-20x compression

questions.explanationMd: Gap encoding reduces the size of document IDs, and variable-byte encoding stores small gaps compactly, giving a typical compression factor around `3-5x` in the lecture data.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, which scenario represents a case where stopword removal should **NOT** be applied?

options.label: A
options.text: A keyword query for a common technical term like `network`

options.label: B
options.text: A phrase query such as `to be or not to be`

options.label: C
options.text: Indexing a large corpus of general news articles

options.label: D
options.text: Preprocessing queries submitted to a web-scale search engine

questions.explanationMd: In phrase queries, stopwords can be essential to the exact phrase. Removing them would change the intended meaning and matching behavior.

questions.questionMd: In gap/delta encoding of a postings list, how is the very first entry in the list stored?

options.label: A
options.text: As the difference between the first and second document IDs

options.label: B
options.text: As the absolute document ID, not as a gap

options.label: C
options.text: As a special sentinel value indicating the beginning of the list

options.label: D
options.text: As a gap of zero to signal the start of the list

questions.explanationMd: The first postings entry has no previous document ID to subtract from, so it is stored as the absolute first document ID.

questions.questionMd: For a single query, the first relevant document appears at rank `3` in the result list. What is the Reciprocal Rank (RR) for this query?
questions.explanationMd: Reciprocal Rank is `1 / rank_of_first_relevant_result`, so `1 / 3 = 0.333...`, approximately `0.33`.

questions.questionMd: A ranked list has graded relevance scores `[3, 1, 0, 2, 1]` at ranks `1` through `5`. What is the approximate `DCG@5`?

options.label: B
options.text: 2.500, computed as the arithmetic mean of the five relevance grades

options.label: C
options.text: 7.000, computed by summing the raw relevance grades `3 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 1`

options.label: D
options.text: 3.000, because only the first rank contributes and its grade is 3

questions.explanationMd: DCG discounts relevance by rank using a logarithmic denominator. The listed calculation gives approximately `4.879`.

questions.questionMd: Which 1960s development is credited as the first systematic, reproducible evaluation of IR systems, establishing the methodology of using test collections and relevance judgments?

options.label: A
options.text: The launch of MEDLARS at the National Library of Medicine

options.label: B
options.text: The introduction of Luhn's automatic keyword extraction

options.label: C
options.text: The SMART system developed by Salton at Cornell

options.label: D
options.text: The Cranfield experiments

questions.explanationMd: The Cranfield experiments established the classic evaluation methodology using test collections, queries, and relevance judgments.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, which of the following statements about BM25 scores is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: BM25 scores are ordinal relevance estimates and should not be compared across different queries

options.label: B
options.text: BM25 scores are symmetric, meaning the score for query Q against document D equals the score for D against Q

options.label: C
options.text: BM25 scores always fall within the range `[0, 1]` because the IDF component is bounded by `log(N)`

options.label: D
options.text: BM25 scores are calibrated probabilities that sum to 1 across all documents for a given query

questions.explanationMd: BM25 scores are useful for ranking documents for the same query, but their numeric values are not calibrated probabilities and should not be compared directly across different queries.

questions.questionMd: In the Boolean retrieval model, what does a query return?

options.label: A
options.text: A probability distribution over matching documents

options.label: B
options.text: A set of document IDs sorted by term frequency

options.label: C
options.text: A ranked list of documents sorted by relevance score

options.label: D
options.text: A set of document IDs with no ordering or relevance scores

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval returns the documents that satisfy the Boolean expression; it does not inherently rank them by relevance.

questions.questionMd: An Elasticsearch deployment uses the `english` language analyzer. Based on the lecture content, which stemming algorithm does this analyzer apply by default?

options.label: A
options.text: WordNet lemmatization

options.label: B
options.text: Lancaster stemming

options.label: C
options.text: Snowball multilingual stemming

options.label: D
options.text: Porter stemming

questions.explanationMd: The lecture identifies the English analyzer's stemming behavior with Porter-style stemming.

questions.questionMd: A new retrieval system retrieves a highly relevant document that was not included in the TREC judgment pool. How does this affect the system's measured evaluation score?

options.label: A
options.text: The document receives the highest relevance grade automatically, rewarding novel retrieval

options.label: B
options.text: The document is treated as irrelevant because it was never judged, which unfairly penalizes the system

options.label: C
options.text: The evaluation is restarted with an expanded pool that includes the new system's results

options.label: D
options.text: The document is excluded from the metric computation, leaving the system's score unchanged

questions.explanationMd: In pooled evaluation, unjudged documents are often treated as nonrelevant, which can unfairly penalize systems that retrieve relevant documents outside the pool.

questions.questionMd: What is the primary reason that lemmatization requires Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging to work correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: POS tagging is needed to filter out stopwords before lemmatization begins

options.label: B
options.text: The same word form can have different base forms depending on its grammatical role

options.label: C
options.text: Lemmatization uses a dictionary that is indexed by POS tag rather than by word form

options.label: D
options.text: Without POS tagging, lemmatization cannot distinguish between nouns and proper nouns

questions.explanationMd: The correct lemma can depend on the word's grammatical role, so POS information helps choose the right base form.

questions.questionMd: A corpus has `N = 100,000` tokens. Using Heap's Law with `k = 44` and `β = 0.49`, what is the approximate predicted vocabulary size?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 100,000 unique terms

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 4,400 unique terms

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 13,600 unique terms

options.label: D
options.text: Approximately 44,000 unique terms

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law estimates vocabulary size as `V = kN^β`. With the lecture's rounded values, this is closest to approximately `13,600` unique terms.

questions.questionMd: On a log-log plot of term rank vs. term frequency, what shape does Zipf's Law predict?

options.label: A
options.text: A straight line with a positive slope

options.label: B
options.text: A concave curve that levels off as rank increases

options.label: C
options.text: An S-shaped logistic curve

options.label: D
options.text: A straight line with a slope of approximately `-1`

questions.explanationMd: Zipf's Law says frequency is roughly inversely proportional to rank, which appears as a straight line with slope about `-1` on a log-log plot.

questions.questionMd: When constructing an 11-point interpolated Precision-Recall curve, how is interpolated Precision defined at a given recall level `r`?

options.label: A
options.text: The minimum Precision across all recall levels `r' > r`, to represent a pessimistic bound

options.label: B
options.text: The Precision value recorded the first time recall `r` is reached during retrieval

options.label: C
options.text: The arithmetic mean of Precision values immediately before and after recall level `r`

options.label: D
options.text: The maximum Precision achieved at any recall level `r'` that is greater than or equal to `r`

questions.explanationMd: Interpolated Precision at recall `r` is the maximum Precision observed for any recall level at least as large as `r`.

questions.questionMd: Three terms are compared for VB compression efficiency: a high-frequency term appearing in `45` documents, a medium-frequency term in `15` documents, and a rare term in `3` documents. Which achieves the highest compression ratio and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The medium-frequency term, because it balances gap size and postings list length optimally

options.label: B
options.text: The high-frequency term

options.label: C
options.text: All three achieve identical compression ratios because VB encoding is independent of term frequency

options.label: D
options.text: The rare term, because fewer postings entries means less data to compress overall

questions.explanationMd: High-frequency terms tend to have smaller gaps between document IDs, so VB encoding can represent their gap values more compactly relative to raw `int32` storage.

questions.questionMd: Why is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test generally preferred over the paired t-test for comparing per-query AP score distributions in IR experiments?

options.label: A
options.text: Wilcoxon directly optimizes NDCG, making it more aligned with the evaluation objective than the t-test

options.label: B
options.text: Wilcoxon is always more statistically powerful than the t-test, producing lower p-values on the same data

options.label: C
options.text: The paired t-test requires at least 1,000 queries to produce valid results, while Wilcoxon works on any sample size

options.label: D
options.text: Wilcoxon is non-parametric and does not assume that per-query score differences are normally distributed

questions.explanationMd: Wilcoxon signed-rank is non-parametric, so it is often preferred when per-query score differences are not normally distributed.

questions.questionMd: A proximity query is written as `term1 /k term2`. Which condition must hold in a candidate document for it to be included in the result?

options.label: A
options.text: The total count of `term1` and `term2` occurrences in the document must equal `k`

options.label: B
options.text: The positional difference between `term1` and `term2` must be at most `k`

options.label: C
options.text: `term1` must appear exactly `k` positions before `term2` in every occurrence

options.label: D
options.text: The terms must appear in the same sentence and within `k` paragraphs of each other

questions.explanationMd: A proximity query requires the terms to occur within a distance threshold `k` according to their positions in the document.

questions.questionMd: During an AND merge with skip pointers, under what condition should the pointer in list `P1` jump to the skip target rather than stepping forward by one?

options.label: A
options.text: When the value at the skip target position in `P1` is strictly less than the current value in `P2`

options.label: B
options.text: When the current value in `P1` is greater than the current value in `P2`

options.label: C
options.text: When the value at the skip target position in `P1` is less than or equal to the current value in `P2`

options.label: D
options.text: When the skip target is within `√|P1|` positions of the current index in `P1`

questions.explanationMd: In postings intersection, a skip is useful when the skip target does not pass beyond the current document ID in the other list; otherwise the algorithm may skip over a possible match.

questions.questionMd: What is the Levenshtein edit distance between `information` and `inforstion`?
questions.explanationMd: Transforming `information` into `inforstion` requires deleting `m` and `a`, so the edit distance is `2`.

questions.questionMd: The sentence `The cat sat on the mat` contains how many tokens and how many types respectively?

options.label: A
options.text: 6 tokens and 6 types

options.label: B
options.text: 5 tokens and 5 types

options.label: C
options.text: 5 tokens and 6 types

options.label: D
options.text: 6 tokens and 5 types

questions.explanationMd: There are six token occurrences, but `the` appears twice after case folding, so there are five unique types.

questions.questionMd: What retrieval behavior results when the BM25 parameter `k1` is set to `0`?

options.label: A
options.text: The IDF component dominates entirely and term frequency is weighted at its maximum possible value

options.label: B
options.text: The TF component becomes binary - only whether a term is present matters, not how many times it appears

options.label: C
options.text: Length normalization is disabled because the denominator reduces to the raw term frequency

options.label: D
options.text: The BM25 score becomes equivalent to raw TF multiplied by IDF with no saturation

questions.explanationMd: When `k1 = 0`, the term-frequency saturation component no longer grows with repeated occurrences; presence/absence dominates.

questions.questionMd: The two-pointer AND merge achieves `O(m + n)` time complexity only because of one crucial property of postings lists. What is that property?

options.label: A
options.text: Postings lists are stored in order of decreasing term frequency

options.label: B
options.text: Postings lists use variable-byte encoded gaps between document IDs

options.label: C
options.text: Postings lists contain positional information for each document

options.label: D
options.text: Postings lists are stored in sorted order of document ID

questions.explanationMd: The linear two-pointer intersection algorithm depends on postings lists being sorted by document ID.

questions.questionMd: A search engineer notices that a document is ranked lower than expected. Which OpenSearch tool would help them understand exactly why that document received its specific relevance score?

options.label: A
options.text: The profile API, which identifies which query clause is the bottleneck causing slow response times

options.label: B
options.text: The `_analyze` API, which shows how the query string is tokenized by the analyzer before matching

options.label: C
options.text: The explain API, which returns the per-term BM25 score breakdown for a specific document

options.label: D
options.text: The `_stats` API, which returns index-level statistics including total document count and segment information

questions.explanationMd: The explain API shows how the score for a specific document was computed, including term-level scoring contributions.

questions.questionMd: In SPIMI, why is only the dictionary key set sorted once per block rather than sorting all `(term, doc_id)` pairs as BSBI does?

options.label: A
options.text: SPIMI uses integer term IDs that are already numerically sorted, eliminating the need to sort strings

options.label: B
options.text: Document IDs are appended in document-processing order directly to each term's list

options.label: C
options.text: Sorting is deferred entirely to the final merge phase, which processes pairs from all blocks simultaneously

options.label: D
options.text: SPIMI processes each document twice: once to assign term IDs and once to sort the pairs

questions.explanationMd: SPIMI builds postings lists directly in memory; as documents are processed in order, document IDs can be appended to each term's postings list without sorting every pair.

questions.questionMd: A rare term appears in only one shard of a 5-shard OpenSearch index. Without any correction, how does this affect BM25 scoring for that term?

options.label: A
options.text: The term is excluded from scoring because OpenSearch requires a term to appear on at least two shards to be indexed

options.label: B
options.text: The shard containing that term computes an artificially high IDF because its local document count is much smaller than the global total

options.label: C
options.text: The term is assigned a zero IDF score because the coordinating node cannot find it on all shards simultaneously

options.label: D
options.text: The term receives a lower-than-global IDF because each shard divides its local IDF by the total number of shards

questions.explanationMd: If IDF is computed locally per shard, a rare term can receive an inflated IDF on the shard where it appears because the local collection statistics are smaller than the global index statistics.

questions.questionMd: System A has `MAP = 0.42` and System B has `MAP = 0.43`. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test yields `p = 0.21`. What is the correct conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: System B is statistically and practically superior because it has a higher MAP score

options.label: B
options.text: The difference is not statistically significant

options.label: C
options.text: System A is preferred because `p > 0.05` confirms its stability across queries

options.label: D
options.text: The test is invalid because the MAP difference is smaller than the p-value

questions.explanationMd: A p-value of `0.21` is above common significance thresholds such as `0.05`, so the observed difference is not statistically significant.

questions.questionMd: A student runs a Porter stemmer and observes that both `universe` and `university` produce the stem `univers`. This is an example of which failure mode?

options.label: A
options.text: Under-stemming, which reduces retrieval recall

options.label: B
options.text: Over-stemming, which reduces retrieval precision

options.label: C
options.text: Incorrect case folding applied before stemming

options.label: D
options.text: Accent folding, which merges morphologically unrelated forms

questions.explanationMd: Over-stemming occurs when different concepts are reduced to the same stem, potentially increasing false matches and reducing precision.

questions.questionMd: Why is cosine similarity preferred over the raw dot product for ranking documents in the Vector Space Model?

options.label: A
options.text: Cosine similarity produces scores in the range `[-1, 1]` while dot products are unbounded

options.label: B
options.text: Cosine similarity normalizes for document length, preventing longer documents from automatically scoring higher than shorter, more focused ones

options.label: C
options.text: Cosine similarity is faster to compute than the dot product for large sparse vectors

options.label: D
options.text: Cosine similarity accounts for term order, while the dot product does not

questions.explanationMd: Cosine similarity divides by vector lengths, reducing the bias that raw dot product has toward longer documents.

questions.questionMd: In Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG), relevance scores are divided by the log base-2 of `(rank + 1)`. What user behavior does this logarithmic discount model?

options.label: A
options.text: Users read results in random order, so position should have no effect on contribution

options.label: B
options.text: Users prefer documents that are only marginally relevant at high ranks over highly relevant documents at low ranks

options.label: C
options.text: User attention diminishes at lower ranks, so a relevant document at rank 10 is worth less than one at rank 1

options.label: D
options.text: The discount penalizes systems that retrieve more than `k` documents, keeping result sets short

questions.explanationMd: DCG discounts lower-ranked results because users are less likely to examine them and their contribution should be smaller.

questions.questionMd:
Given the documents below, which postings list is correct for the term `cat`?

`Doc 0: "the cat sat on the mat"`

`Doc 1: "the cat ate the rat"`

`Doc 2: "the rat sat and ate"`

options.label: A
options.text: Doc 0 and Doc 1

options.label: B
options.text: Doc 0 and Doc 2

options.label: C
options.text: Doc 1 and Doc 2

options.label: D
options.text: Doc 0, Doc 1, and Doc 2

questions.explanationMd: The term `cat` appears in Doc 0 and Doc 1, but not in Doc 2.

questions.questionMd: Compared to the original forward dictionary, approximately how much larger does the permuterm index grow?

options.label: A
options.text: Roughly 2 times larger

options.label: B
options.text: The same size, since rotations are stored as pointers rather than full strings

options.label: C
options.text: Roughly 10 times larger

options.label: D
options.text: Roughly 4 to 5 times larger

questions.explanationMd: A permuterm index stores rotations of terms, making it several times larger than the original dictionary; the lecture's approximate figure is `4-5x`.

questions.questionMd: What is the key architectural difference between the BSBI and SPIMI index construction algorithms?

options.label: A
options.text: SPIMI sorts all term-document pairs before writing any block to disk, while BSBI does not

options.label: B
options.text: BSBI requires a global term-to-integer mapping across all blocks, while SPIMI does not

options.label: C
options.text: BSBI writes sorted postings directly to disk, while SPIMI keeps all postings in RAM permanently

options.label: D
options.text: BSBI is designed for single-pass processing, while SPIMI requires multiple passes over the corpus

questions.explanationMd: BSBI sorts termID-documentID pairs and depends on a global mapping, while SPIMI builds term dictionaries and postings directly within each block.

questions.questionMd: Variable-byte (VB) encoding uses a continuation bit within each byte. What does a continuation bit value of `1` (the top bit set) indicate in VB encoding?

options.label: A
options.text: This byte encodes a negative gap and should be subtracted

options.label: B
options.text: This byte is a continuation byte and more bytes follow for the current number

options.label: C
options.text: This byte marks the boundary between two separate encoded numbers

options.label: D
options.text: This is the last terminal byte of the current encoded number

questions.explanationMd: In the lecture's VB convention, the top bit set to `1` marks the final byte of the current encoded number.

questions.questionMd: A term has a document frequency (DF) of `500` and a term frequency (TF) of `12` in one particular document. What does the DF value of `500` indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: The term appears in documents with an average length of 500 tokens

options.label: B
options.text: The term appears in 500 different documents in the corpus

options.label: C
options.text: The term's postings list contains 500 position entries

options.label: D
options.text: The term appears 500 times across all documents combined

questions.explanationMd: Document frequency is the number of documents in which a term occurs.

questions.questionMd: A preprocessing pipeline applies Porter stemming to the phrase query `space shuttle` before executing a positional phrase query. What stems does Porter produce for these two words, and why must the same stemming be applied to both queries and documents?

options.label: A
options.text: Porter produces `["space", "shuttl"]`; both sides must match so that query terms align with indexed terms

options.label: B
options.text: Porter produces `["spac", "shuttle"]`; only documents need stemming because queries are already normalized

options.label: C
options.text: Porter produces `["space", "shuttle"]`; stemming does not affect short dictionary words

options.label: D
options.text: Porter produces `["spac", "shuttl"]`; documents are stemmed but queries use raw tokens for higher precision

questions.explanationMd: Stemming must be applied consistently to both indexed documents and queries so phrase terms match the same normalized token forms.

questions.questionMd: In IR system design, Boolean retrieval and neural reranking sit at opposite ends of a fundamental tradeoff. Which pair of terms correctly names the two competing goals?

options.label: A
options.text: Index compression versus index coverage

options.label: B
options.text: Efficiency (speed and scale) versus effectiveness (accuracy and relevance)

options.label: C
options.text: Precision (result quality) versus recall (result completeness)

options.label: D
options.text: Offline processing versus online processing

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval emphasizes efficient exact matching at scale, while neural reranking often improves effectiveness at higher computational cost.

questions.questionMd: In a positional index, what specific information is stored for each term-document pair that is absent from a basic inverted index?

options.label: A
options.text: The positions/offsets of each token occurrence within the document

options.label: B
options.text: The document frequency of the term across the entire corpus

options.label: C
options.text: The term frequency of each token normalized by document length

options.label: D
options.text: The byte offset of the document in the original corpus file

questions.explanationMd: A positional index stores where each occurrence of a term appears in a document, enabling phrase and proximity queries.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a fundamental limitation of the Boolean retrieval model?

options.label: A
options.text: Results cannot be cached because they change with each query

options.label: B
options.text: A document that satisfies all but one query term is excluded entirely from results

options.label: C
options.text: The model cannot support the NOT operator on large corpora

options.label: D
options.text: Query processing time scales quadratically with the number of query terms

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval applies exact logical conditions; a document that misses one required term may be excluded even if it is otherwise highly relevant.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch query uses `"fields": ["title^3", "body^1"]` inside a `multi_match` clause. What does the `^3` notation mean for the `title` field?

options.label: A
options.text: A match in the title field contributes three times more to the relevance score than an equivalent match in the body field

options.label: B
options.text: The title field is indexed three times to increase recall for title matches

options.label: C
options.text: The query requires at least three matching terms in the title field before the document is considered a candidate

options.label: D
options.text: OpenSearch searches the title field three times before falling back to the body field

questions.explanationMd: The `^3` syntax boosts matches in the `title` field so they contribute more heavily than matches in lower-weighted fields.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a key advantage of the Snowball stemmer over the original Porter stemmer?

options.label: A
options.text: Snowball always produces real dictionary words as output, unlike Porter

options.label: B
options.text: Snowball provides multilingual support for languages

options.label: C
options.text: Snowball uses a morphological lexicon instead of rule-based suffix removal

options.label: D
options.text: Snowball applies more aggressive suffix stripping, achieving a smaller vocabulary

questions.explanationMd: Snowball generalizes stemming algorithms and provides support for multiple languages.

questions.questionMd: Which statement most accurately captures the definition of Information Retrieval as a discipline?

options.label: A
options.text: Executing structured queries against relational database tables to return exact matching rows

options.label: B
options.text: Automatically discovering hidden patterns and clusters across large numerical datasets

options.label: C
options.text: Annotating natural language text with grammatical and semantic labels for downstream processing

options.label: D
options.text: Finding relevant information resources from a collection in response to an information need

questions.explanationMd: Information Retrieval focuses on finding relevant information resources that satisfy a user's information need.

questions.questionMd: In an OpenSearch cluster, which node type is responsible for receiving a client search request, routing it to the appropriate shards, and merging the results before returning them to the client?

options.label: A
options.text: The coordinating node

options.label: B
options.text: The primary data node that holds the most shards

options.label: C
options.text: The replica node designated as the query leader for that request

options.label: D
options.text: The master node

questions.explanationMd: The coordinating node receives the client request, distributes work to shards, merges shard results, and returns the final response.

questions.questionMd: Which formula correctly defines the F1 score in terms of Precision (`P`) and Recall (`R`)?

options.label: C
options.text: `PR / (P + R)`

questions.explanationMd: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: `2PR / (P + R)`.

questions.questionMd: In OpenSearch's two-phase query execution model, what does the coordinating node do during the fetch phase?

options.label: A
options.text: It broadcasts the query to all shards and waits for each shard to score its local documents

options.label: B
options.text: It selects the global top-k documents by merging shard scores, then retrieves from the relevant shards

options.label: C
options.text: It writes the query result to a distributed cache so that repeated queries are served without contacting the shards again

options.label: D
options.text: It collects global term statistics from every shard before any scoring takes place

questions.explanationMd: After shard-level scoring, the coordinating node determines the global top results and fetches the corresponding documents from the relevant shards.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following best explains why simple whitespace tokenization is insufficient for production search systems?

options.label: A
options.text: It always produces more tokens than a regex-based tokenizer would for the same input

options.label: B
options.text: It fails to handle contractions, possessives, URLs, and hyphenated expressions correctly

options.label: C
options.text: It requires an external dictionary to identify valid word boundaries

options.label: D
options.text: It is too slow for large corpora because it scans the entire text character by character

questions.explanationMd: Production tokenizers must handle many linguistic and web-specific cases that whitespace splitting cannot model reliably.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, a biword index stores every consecutive pair of terms as a single index entry. What is the primary drawback of this approach compared to a positional index?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be combined with stopword removal because bigrams containing stopwords must be retained

options.label: B
options.text: It requires storing token positions for every document, making it 2-4 times larger than a basic inverted index

options.label: C
options.text: Vocabulary size grows quadratically, from `N` terms to potentially `N²` bigrams, and it cannot support arbitrary phrase lengths

options.label: D
options.text: It is slower to build than a positional index because every bigram must be stemmed separately

questions.explanationMd: Biword indexes can greatly expand the vocabulary and support only fixed-length adjacent pairs rather than arbitrary phrase/proximity queries.

questions.questionMd: Zipf's Law states that the frequency of the `r`-th most common word is proportional to `1/r`. If the most frequent term in a corpus appears `10,000` times, approximately how often does the `100`th most frequent term appear?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 10 times

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 100 times

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 1,000 times

options.label: D
options.text: Approximately 5,000 times

questions.explanationMd: Using `frequency ≈ 10000 / r`, the 100th ranked term appears about `10000 / 100 = 100` times.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a fundamental limitation of Boolean retrieval that motivates the move to ranked retrieval?

options.label: A
options.text: Boolean retrieval cannot use an inverted index to look up postings lists

options.label: B
options.text: Boolean retrieval is unable to handle OR operators between query terms

options.label: C
options.text: Boolean retrieval requires all query terms to be stemmed before matching

options.label: D
options.text: A document matching 3 out of 4 query terms is treated the same as one matching 0 terms if the Boolean condition is not satisfied

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval lacks graded relevance; documents that partly match a query may receive no credit if they fail the exact Boolean condition.

questions.questionMd: What is the core intuition behind Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) as used in TF-IDF weighting?

options.label: A
options.text: Terms that appear in many documents are more likely to be relevant to any query

options.label: B
options.text: IDF increases the weight of terms that co-occur with stopwords

options.label: C
options.text: IDF penalizes terms based on how frequently they appear within a single document

options.label: D
options.text: Terms that appear in many documents carry little discriminating information and should receive lower weights

questions.explanationMd: IDF assigns lower weight to common terms because they are less useful for distinguishing relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: According to the length normalization worked example in the lecture notes, when two documents contain a query term the same number of times but differ in length, how does BM25 treat the shorter document?

options.label: A
options.text: The shorter document receives a lower TF saturation score because BM25 penalizes documents with few total tokens

options.label: B
options.text: The shorter document receives a higher TF saturation score because its length is below average, signaling greater topical focus

options.label: C
options.text: The shorter document is excluded from ranking because BM25 requires a minimum document length relative to `avgdl`

options.label: D
options.text: Both documents receive identical TF saturation scores because BM25 only compares document length to `k1`, not to `avgdl`

questions.explanationMd: BM25 length normalization rewards a query term occurring in a shorter document more strongly than the same frequency in a longer document.

questions.questionMd: Case folding converts `Apple` to `apple` during normalization. According to the lecture, which specific example demonstrates that lowercasing is **NOT** always a safe operation?

options.label: A
options.text: `Running` and `running` should always be treated as the same term

options.label: B
options.text: Accent folding should always be performed before case folding

options.label: C
options.text: `Apple` (company name) vs. `apple` (the fruit) carry different meanings

options.label: D
options.text: `NASA` should always be lowercased to `nasa` for consistency

questions.explanationMd: Case can carry semantic information; `Apple` as a company and `apple` as a fruit are not always interchangeable.

questions.questionMd: A basic inverted index returns documents containing both `space` and `shuttle` using an AND operation, but includes a document where these words appear far apart and in a different order. What type of index is needed to eliminate such false positives?

options.label: A
options.text: A biword index that stores every adjacent pair of terms as a single entry

options.label: B
options.text: A term-frequency index that weights terms by how often they co-occur

options.label: C
options.text: A compressed index that uses gap encoding to reduce postings list size

options.label: D
options.text: A positional index that stores token positions within each document

questions.explanationMd: A positional index can verify term order and distance, allowing exact phrase and proximity matching.

questions.questionMd: Why does the smoothed IDF formula `log(N / (df + 1)) + 1` add `1` to the denominator?

options.label: A
options.text: To ensure that every term receives an IDF value greater than 1 regardless of collection size

options.label: B
options.text: To bring the IDF range into alignment with the range produced by log-TF

options.label: C
options.text: To make very common terms receive a higher IDF than they would under the standard formula

options.label: D
options.text: To prevent division by zero when a term has never appeared in any document in the collection

questions.explanationMd: Adding `1` to `df` prevents division by zero for unseen terms and is a common smoothing technique.

questions.questionMd: Crawling, text preprocessing, and index construction are all classified as offline pipeline stages. What is the primary architectural reason for this design choice?

options.label: A
options.text: Building the index in advance allows online query processing to complete within strict millisecond latency budgets

options.label: B
options.text: Online stages require specialized hardware that cannot also execute indexing workloads

options.label: C
options.text: Preprocessing must be performed after each user query to reflect the most recent document versions

options.label: D
options.text: Offline stages consume too much RAM to run concurrently with live query traffic

questions.explanationMd: Expensive document processing and index construction are done offline so online query serving can be fast.

questions.questionMd: A system administrator doubles the number of replica shards in an OpenSearch cluster that is under heavy read load. Which outcome is most directly expected?

options.label: A
options.text: Read throughput increases because more shards can serve search requests concurrently

options.label: B
options.text: Query relevance scores improve because IDF is now computed using a larger combined document pool

options.label: C
options.text: Indexing latency decreases because replicas process new documents in parallel with the primary

options.label: D
options.text: Write throughput increases because documents are now distributed across more physical locations

questions.explanationMd: Replica shards can serve read/search requests, so adding replicas can improve read throughput under heavy search load.
